title: Grade 11 Physics — Laws of Motion & Work, Energy and Power
description: Laws of Motion and Work Energy and Power practice questions
subject: physics

questions.question: A body of mass 5 kg is acted on by a force of 20 N. The acceleration produced is:
A passenger in a suddenly braking car is thrown forward due to:
questions.explanation: When the car brakes, the passenger's body continues moving forward (inertia of motion) while the car decelerates. This is Newton's first law in action.

questions.question: The coefficient of static friction is generally:
questions.explanation: Static friction (maximum) ≥ kinetic friction. It takes more force to start an object moving than to keep it moving. So μₛ > μₖ typically.

questions.question: A 10 kg block is on a frictionless surface. If a 50 N force is applied, the block's acceleration is:
The force required to keep an object of mass m moving in a circle of radius r at speed v is:
questions.explanation: Centripetal force = mv²/r. It is always directed toward the centre of the circle.

questions.question: When a horse pulls a cart, by Newton's third law, the cart pulls the horse with equal and opposite force. Why does the cart still move?
options: The forces act on different objects; the net force on the cart (from horse minus friction) is non-zero
The third law doesn't apply here
questions.explanation: Action-reaction forces act on different objects. For the cart: horse pulls it forward, ground friction acts backward. If the forward pull exceeds friction, the net force on the cart is forward, and it accelerates.

questions.question: The maximum safe speed of a vehicle on a banked circular road of radius r, banking angle θ, is:
questions.explanation: On a banked road without friction: v_max = √(rg tan θ). Banking allows vehicles to take turns at higher speeds without relying on friction.

questions.question: Impulse equals:
questions.explanation: Impulse J = F × t = Δp (change in momentum). This is an application of Newton's second law: F = dp/dt → F×dt = dp.

questions.question: Work done W when force F is applied at angle θ to displacement d is:
questions.explanation: W = F·d cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. If θ = 0° (force along displacement), W = Fd. If θ = 90°, W = 0.

questions.question: The kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving at velocity v is:
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv². This is derived from the work-energy theorem: W = ΔKE.

questions.question: The work-energy theorem states:
options: Work done by net force = change in kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE. The net work done by all forces on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy.

questions.question: Power is defined as:
options: Rate of doing work (work per unit time)
questions.explanation: Power P = W/t = rate of doing work. SI unit is Watt (W = J/s). Also P = F·v (force × velocity) for constant force.

questions.question: Conservation of mechanical energy states that in the absence of non-conservative forces:
questions.explanation: In the absence of friction and other non-conservative forces, the total mechanical energy (KE + PE) of a system remains constant.

questions.question: An elastic collision conserves:
questions.explanation: Elastic collision: both kinetic energy and momentum are conserved. In an inelastic collision, only momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is partially lost.

questions.question: A spring with spring constant k is compressed by x. The potential energy stored is:
questions.explanation: Elastic potential energy = ½kx², where k is spring constant and x is the compression/extension from natural length.
